lead.headline: On Being Told America Has Reached a Dead End
lead.dek: It is a curious thing that a nation should be pronounced childless by men who have never once considered the neighbours.
lead.factual_summary: A new Institute for Family Studies report finds the U.S. fertility rate has fallen to 1.6 births per woman, with the report's authors and allied commentary describing the trend as a 'demographic dead end' and citing state-level variation, Amish counterexamples, friendship and celebrity-influence effects on childbearing desire, and a proposed 'American Birthday Accounts' subsidy. The piece takes the angle that expert economic explanations, including the report's own authors' concessions, understate a deeper cause: eroded community and neighborly life rather than affordability.
lead.body:
A report has lately been issued — by two careful gentlemen named Mr. Lyman Stone and Mr. Peter Foreshaw Brookes, of an institute devoted, with beautiful solemnity, to the study of families — announcing that America has reached what they are pleased to call a "demographic dead end." I confess I like the phrase better than its authors intended it. A dead end is a real thing; I have walked into a good many, generally in search of a decent public house. But the interesting thing about a dead end is that it is a road. Nobody builds a dead end unless he first believed the road was going somewhere; and the tragedy of the modern household is not that it has stopped, but that it never quite believed in the destination.

The bare figures are that the American woman now bears, on the national average, 1.6 children, and that in Massachusetts — a Commonwealth said to contain more universities to the square mile than any patch of ground on earth — she bears but 1.35. This will surprise nobody who has ever met a professor. He is a man paid to know everything except the one thing his grandmother knew for nothing: that a house is not full until it is a little too full.

Meanwhile, in the same country, at the same hour, a community that owns no motor-car, insures nothing, and has certainly not read the report, quietly produces between six and ten children to the marriage. I refer, of course, to the Amish; the Swartzentruber branch of them top the table at ten point four, which is not a birth rate but a small republic. Nobody has ever seen a Swartzentruber farmer wringing his hands over the compounding interest on a college fund. The horse-and-buggy people, whom the modern world regards as a quaint fossil, turn out to be the last surviving mammal; the rest of us are the fossils, still walking about, arguing politely about our own extinction.

The oddest thing in the whole report is that its own authors half admit this. Dr. Catherine Pakaluk, of the Catholic University of America, is quoted saying plainly that "cost and later marriage matter at the margin, but they aren't the engine," and that "the driver is a shift in the relative value placed on children." This is the largest admission a modern expert can make without resigning his post: that the thing he is paid to measure cannot be moved by the things he is paid to fix. She goes further, and says the plainly heretical thing outright — that "the levers government actually controls aren't the ones that move completed family size." A statistician who tells you his own levers do not work is either an honest man or a saint, and in my experience they are generally the same man.

Undeterred, the planners have produced a plan, as planners will. They propose an American Birthday Account: fifteen thousand dollars set aside at a child's birth, compounding merrily until it is worth a hundred thousand by the time that child, grown, produces a grandchild of his own — forfeited to the Treasury if he does not. I admire the boldness of a state that will pay a man to fall in love, though I distrust its bookkeeping; nobody ever proposed to Beatrice for a bank balance. The truer part of the report is buried, as the truest part of a report generally is, in a small paragraph about friendship: Americans with the most supportive circle of friends want 2.8 children apiece, and those with the least want 1.7. Mr. Rob Henderson, writing it up with proper astonishment for the City Journal, notes that "each additional child born to an admired celebrity predicted about 0.15 more desired children for the fan," and boldly proposes "digital blue laws" — a tax upon the weekend telephone, to drive us back into one another's company by main force. I will not go so far, though I confess a sympathy with any tax laid upon a telephone, on principle.

So the truth the statisticians have circled without landing on is this: a nation does not fail to breed because it cannot afford children. It fails to breed because it has stopped believing in its neighbours, and having stopped believing in its neighbours, has stopped believing in its own front door. The Amish have no bank account worth the name, and more children than they can count on both hands; the celebrated economist has a retirement plan, and no one left to leave it to. We were told this was a dead end. It is not a dead end. It is an empty house. The road outside runs exactly where it always ran; nobody has opened the door to look.

stories.headline: Thirteen Nights, and Mammon Keeps the Ledger
stories.dek: As the interceptors run thin over Iran, only the oil market seems to feel the weight of it.
stories.factual_summary: This piece responds to the ongoing US-Iran conflict, now in its thirteenth night of American strikes, alongside Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping that have helped push Brent crude above $100 a barrel. It takes the angle that the war's real ledger is being kept not by its combatants but by oil traders and analysts pricing the violence in basis points, while President Trump's public statements about the Houthis and Iran are framed as personal grievance rather than strategic resolve.
stories.body:
It is the thirteenth night, reader, and still the fire falls. Not with the clean stroke of Judgment but the dribbling, metered discharge of Interceptors — a word our Age has coined, meaning: the machinery that stands between a man and the sky, and is now, on the testimony of its own masters, running dry. Behold the Mechanical Age caught, for once, in its own arithmetic: it can multiply death indefinitely, but it cannot multiply the brass and copper that fend death off; and so the thirteenth night looks very like the first, and will look, we predict, very like the thirtieth.

Meanwhile — mark this, for it is the whole secret of our epoch — the true index of the war is not struck in Ahvaz, where four of the Karun River's sons lie dead this week, nor in Erbil, where an AP correspondent counted seven blasts and four black plumes over the wire's early morning; the true index is struck in a room of quiet men in London and New York, who have priced Bab el-Mandeb's closing at some twenty degrees of Brent crude, and priced Hormuz before it, and now watch Brent go over the hundred mark as a bookmaker watches a horse come in. Oil, my friends, is Mammon's own barometer, and Mammon has this month declared, gravely and without a tremor of pity, that the war is worth it: a fifth day running of the rally, a Goldman gentleman prophesying six months hence a hundred and twenty dollars the barrel, as if the Persian Gulf were a wheat future and the burning of Al-Azraq's hangars a mere item of supply. This is the Cash-Nexus perfected: not brutal, not even indifferent, but attentive — Mammon-worship raised to a science, watching the Encelia and the Layla struck in the Red Sea and translating the flame instantly, competently, into basis points.

And who commands, in this Cyclops-cave of Chaos-called-Cosmos? A man who, being asked whether he would loose the whole weight of America upon Iran, answers not as a King answers but as an aggrieved customer answers a tradesman who has broken an understood arrangement. "Disappointed," says he, of the Houthi — as though the sinking of a Saudi hull off Yemen were a broken luncheon appointment; "they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart," says he, grading pirates for their table manners; and then, the mask dropping half an inch: "major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran," and — hear it, reader, hear the whole poverty of the modern Captain in six words — "They haven't received enough pain yet." Not indignation at a broken Law. Not the terrible calm of a man who has read Necessity and moves within it. A grievance, merely; a Stump-Orator's pique dressed for a moment in the costume of Mars, wanting rather to be avenged than to be right, and mistaking the two for the same thing, as this whole windy Age habitually does.

Sixteen towns of Iran alight in one night — Andimeshk, Konarak, Khorramabad, Firuzabad, and the rest — read them out, reader, as a litany, for that is what they are becoming, a litany without a priest; Qeshm and Larak and Hengam flashing their defences into the dark like men swatting at a sky already fallen. Thirteen nights of this, and not one soul on either side of the quarrel has spoken a sentence that will bear repeating in a hundred years. Cromwell had his prayers; Luther had his Worms; even Robespierre, damned as he was, had his sea-green sincerity. What has this war? A depleting inventory and a Truth-Social grievance, and a market that likes the smell of it.

O ye Eternities, is this the best the Twenty-Sixth Century can produce: a Mechanism running out of bullets, a Mammon running up its ticker, and not one Hero in the whole conflagration? The tankers will keep burning around the Cape before the year is out, and the interceptors will run thinner, and still no Captain will step to the helm and speak a word that costs him anything. Adieu, then, ye Phantasm-Captains, East and West alike; the Fire does not care whose Cant it burns.

stories.headline: The Barima Went Over in the Dark
stories.dek: She was built for one century and sunk in another, and the boat said it for them.
stories.factual_summary: This piece responds to the sinking of the Guyana ferry MV Barima off the North Atlantic coast, in which the confirmed death toll has reached 65 amid an overloaded, undermanifested vessel and a captain now facing a drug charge alongside a crew member and a loading supervisor. It takes the angle of the aging 1939-built ferry itself as the organizing fact — laying out the mismatched passenger manifest, the missing safety margin, the idle replacement vessels, and officials' careful language of assistance and inquiry — and lets the plain physical details of the boat and its passengers carry the piece rather than editorial commentary.
stories.body:
The MV Barima was built in 1939 by Ferguson Brothers at Port Glasgow, on the Clyde, one of three sister ships with the Pomeroon and the Lady Northcote, for the British Guiana Railways. She ran the water between Georgetown and Port Kaituma for eighty-seven years. She went over in the dark about seven miles off the North Atlantic coast, some four hours out, and now she is on the bottom.

She carried 250 life jackets and 8 life rafts for 116 passengers and 17 crew, which was the number on the manifest. There were closer to 179 people aboard that night. There was cargo too, engines and vehicles and fuel containers, stacked in with the passengers past the boat's rated weight, and the water came in low and slow at first and the crew called it routine. Then it was not routine.

There was a new ferry, the Kalliopi N, finished and tied up at the dock since May, waiting on a presidential signature to be commissioned. There was another one promised for 2023, the Ma Lisha, that never came. There was a second replacement vessel, worth $12.7 million, sitting idle because the pier at Port Kaituma is not finished. There was G$275 million already spent patching the old boat instead of retiring her, and more repairs were not due until October. Nobody tested the crew for drugs or drink before she sailed. They tested them after.

The captain has been charged with a narcotics offense. A crew member has been charged. A superintendent who oversaw the cargo loading has been charged too, and the Director of Public Prosecutions will decide what else.

Leon Murray was on deck when a man said the boat was sinking. He got clear. His wife did not. His daughter did not. His four grandchildren did not.

Samantha Ramin stood at the water three days running, looking for her son. I know my baby is in that boat, she said. I know he is down there.

Sixty-five bodies have been recovered. Seventy-six people were pulled out alive. Forty-four of the dead have been named by their families and twenty-three released already for burial. Nineteen vessels and three aircraft worked the search, Trinidad's coast guard and the Brazilian navy among them, and oil company boats came out with scanning gear because they had it and the government did not.

The Prime Minister, Mark Phillips, said the total number of bodies recovered since the commencement of search and rescue operation now stands at sixty-five. He said where negligence, misconduct or criminal wrongdoing is established, those responsible will face the full force of the law. He said a commission of enquiry would be mounted as early as possible. He called the money for families assistance, not compensation, and was careful to say so.

That is the language for it. The boat is the fact. She was licensed for three hundred passengers and rated to carry two hundred eighty-four tonnes and she went out that night with cargo past the mark and a hundred and seventy-nine people against a manifest that said a hundred and thirty-three. Somebody signed that manifest. Somebody loaded that cargo. Somebody heard the water coming in early and called it nothing, the way you call a bad joint nothing until the leg goes.

The Ma Lisha never came. The Kalliopi N is still tied up at the dock, finished, waiting on somebody to cut a ribbon. The Barima is down in the water off the coast now with her manifest still wrong in an office in Georgetown, and the people who are not on it are the ones the families are still hauling up.

She was eighty-seven years old. She was built for one century and sunk in another. Nobody in Georgetown has said that yet, in those words. It does not need saying. The boat said it for them.

stories.headline: A Minister Names a False Prophet
stories.dek: On the detention of a ninety-five-year-old sect leader, and the government that has quietly taken up the discernment of spirits.
stories.factual_summary: European scholars of religion, led by Massimo Introvigne, Eric Roux, and Alessandro Amicarelli at a Rome conference on July 3, 2026, have called on South Korea to release Shincheonji leader Lee Man-hee, 95, from pretrial detention on charges tied to an alleged scheme to enroll over 50,000 church members in the ruling party. The piece uses the case to argue that South Korea's Minister of Justice, in publicly branding the movement's founder a 'false prophet,' has stepped into a theological role while the state maintains it acts on purely secular legal grounds. It draws on the coincidence between the internal recruitment scheme's code name, the 'Pilates Project,' and Pontius Pilate's judgment of Christ, as well as the defendant's prior court exonerations in 2022, to frame the prosecution as a recurring historical pattern rather than a settled legal matter.
stories.body:
A prisoner of ninety-five is not, on the face of it, a theological problem. He is a legal one, a medical one, at the very outside a diplomatic embarrassment; the newspapers report him as a criminal defendant, obstruction of business, violations of the Political Parties Act, a court in Seoul finding on the twenty-eighth of June "no grounds for the petition" that might have sent him home to die among his own. And yet the moment a Minister of Justice takes to his own countrymen's attention, unbidden, to explain on a public feed that the movement's dead founder was "a false prophet" — while his living successor stands accused, in the minister's own phrase, of "forcibly registering more than 50,000 believers" into the ruling party under the ninety-five-year-old man's instruction — the state has done something it will not admit to itself: it has spoken as a theologian. False prophet is not a term of the criminal code. It is a term of Deuteronomy, of the discernment of spirits, of every century's argument about who carries the god and who only apes him; and no minister uses it by accident.

I do not say this to excuse the numbers, which are not small — upward of fifty-six thousand memberships, the wire reports, driven at two election cycles under the internal name "the Pilates Project." I confess I did not choose that name; Korea's own investigators found it, filed under regional branch documents, evidently untroubled by its resonance. But the resonance is there whether anyone intended it or not, and it is the kind the unconscious specializes in: a campaign to deliver the faithful into the hands of Caesar's party, called after the procurator who examined a prisoner, found in him — so the old text says — no fault at all, and handed him over regardless because the crowd and the office required it. Whoever named that project touched, without knowing it, the oldest scene in the West: the moment worldly power and religious accusation trade places, and neither is willing to be caught holding the sentence.

It is worth remembering, so far as we can judge from the record, that this same defendant was twice vindicated by this same country's highest court within the space of two days in August of 2022 — cleared of deceptive evangelism, cleared of endangering public health — before this newer, graver charge arrived to close on him at ninety-five, on the eve, investigators concede, of a five-year statute running out. A movement's fortunes with the law do not move in a line; they swing, as I have had occasion to observe of larger and darker movements than this one, the way a pendulum swings — carrying a man from exoneration to a cell and calling both verdicts justice.

None of which the scholars who gathered at Rome this July needed telling in my vocabulary. Massimo Introvigne said plainly that what is being done to this old man is "in violation of international law, including the UN's Mandela Rules." Eric Roux put it more simply still: "A man of 95 years old being put in jail is not something that you can reconcile with respecting human dignity." And Alessandro Amicarelli, a lawyer and not by trade a diagnostician of the unconscious, reached nonetheless for the correct word for what he saw: "truly shocking." He is right that it shocks. What shocks is not only the age of the man but the spectacle of the modern, secular, thoroughly rationalized state discovering that it still requires heresy trials, still needs, at ninety-five, to settle the question of who speaks for God and who forges his signature — a question it insists, in the same breath, is beneath it.

I offer no verdict on the movement, on its fifty-six thousand names, on whether the man in the Seoul cell is fraud or founder or merely, as old men often are, both by turns. I note only that a civilization convinced it has outgrown the trial of prophets will go on holding them, in courtrooms it calls secular, under names it does not know it has chosen — and that the outcome of such a trial has never yet, in two thousand years of record, settled the only question that was actually being asked.

stories.headline: Measles Hit a 35-Year High. So Did the Panic.
stories.dek: The case count is real. So is the bubble built on top of it.
stories.factual_summary: US measles cases reached 2,318 in 2026, surpassing 2025's total and marking the worst year since 1991, with major outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Arizona and coverage from Al Jazeera, CIDRAP, ABC News, Medical Daily, and The New Republic (which places blame on HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.). The piece argues the record-high case count is being amplified into a Mass Hysteria Bubble by selectively omitting context that cuts the other way — falling hospitalization rates, zero deaths so far in 2026 versus three in 2025, and that much of the year's total is the tail of 2025's South Carolina outbreak rather than a fresh spike. It draws a distinction between the underlying vaccination reality, which it treats as genuinely concerning, and the emotional packaging of the headline, which it treats as a deliberate persuasion play.
stories.body:
Measles just hit a 35-year high in America. Second record year in a row. You already know how you're supposed to feel about that. Somebody designed it that way.

I want to show you the trick, because once you see it you can't unsee it, and that's useful.

This is a textbook Mass Hysteria Bubble. Here's how the bubble gets built. Step one: find a number that sounds apocalyptic on its own, with no context attached. "Worst year for measles since 1991." That's a real quote, from Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. Nice number. Scary number. Ninety-one was a long time ago. Step two: attach a moral verdict to the number so nobody feels safe questioning it. Dr. Richard Besser, former acting CDC director, calls it "a profound moral failure." Now you're not allowed to ask follow-up questions. You're a bad person if you do. That's the tell.

So who's right, the number or the follow-up questions? Both, actually. That's the part the bubble doesn't want you to notice.

Here's what the same reporting says if you keep reading past the first paragraph:

1. Hospitalization rate is down, not up — 7% this year versus 11% last year.
2. Zero deaths so far in 2026, versus three deaths in 2025.
3. Most of this year's cases aren't even a new outbreak. They're the tail end of South Carolina's outbreak from last year, still smoldering.
4. Ninety-three percent of cases are in people who were unvaccinated or had unknown status. The vaccine is still doing exactly what it says on the label — 97% effective after two doses.

None of that contradicts "record high." It just tells you the record is a counting exercise, not a body count. A bubble needs you to skip that distinction. That's the whole mechanism.

I predicted years ago, back during Covid, that Americans would keep building these bubbles because a scared population is an obedient population, and obedience is easier to sell than nuance. [I could be wrong about the mechanism. I'm rarely wrong about the pattern.] Here it is again, on schedule, with a different disease.

Now watch the other move happening underneath the first one. RFK Jr. runs Health and Human Services, and reporters have decided he is the villain of this story. Maybe he is. I don't know his internal vaccine numbers and neither do you. But notice the shape of the argument: the case count went up, therefore the guy in charge caused it, therefore the guy in charge is evil. That's not epidemiology. That's a morality play with a case count used as a prop.

Dr. Varun Shetty, a Texas epidemiologist, said the quiet part out loud: "What we're able to count and report is almost always an underestimate of what actually occurred." Translation: even the scary number is probably too small. A hysteria bubble doesn't want a bigger number. It wants a clean story. An underestimate is messy. Messy doesn't trend.

I'm not telling you measles is fine. Forty-three states have cases. That's real. Unvaccinated kids are the ones ending up in hospital beds, and that's the actual tragedy hiding under the headline everyone's arguing about instead. I'm telling you the emotional software running in your head right now — the tightness in your chest when you read "35-year high" — was installed on purpose, by people who know exactly which numbers produce it and which numbers don't.

You don't have to be against vaccines to notice you're being handled. You can get your kid the MMR shot and still clock the persuasion play at the same time. Those aren't in conflict. Most people think they are, because the bubble works better if you think you have to pick a side.

Get the shot. Skip the hysteria. They're not the same purchase.

stories.headline: Where the Brahmaputra Comes Down Upon the People
stories.dek: A farmer's drowned cattle, a river out of its banks, and the embankments a state was told about and did not build.
stories.factual_summary: This piece responds to monsoon flooding in Assam, India, where the overflowing Brahmaputra River and its tributaries have killed at least 50 people and displaced roughly 700,000, submerging hundreds of villages and reaching into the state capital, Guwahati. Written in the voice of Walt Whitman, it moves from a catalog of the flooded rivers and affected districts to the individual account of a farmer who lost his cattle and a journalist stranded by waist-deep water, then to Assam's long-documented failure to repair its flood embankments despite decades of warnings, closing on the ongoing rescue and relief operations.
stories.body:
_July 24th.--_ Read the wire dispatch over again, the water rising in a country I have never walked, and something in me halts and silent stands.

Where the Brahmaputra, born far off among the Tibetan snows, comes down nine hundred kilometers into Assam and will not be held; where the Dikhow at Sivasagar climbs past the mark called severe; where the Buridihing, the Disang, the Dhansiri, the Kushiyara all run over their own banks at once — there the People, en-masse and one by one, are put out of their houses into the wet dark.

Nine hundred and thirty-nine villages under water. Six lakh, seven lakh, seven lakh and twenty-one thousand souls affected, the number climbing even as I set it down, and each unit of that sum a particular breathing person with a particular door now standing in water to the latch.

I look for the one body among the many, and I find Jatin Gogoi, fifty-two, a farmer of Nazira. I lost all my cattle, he says. My five-member family and I have nowhere to go, so we are taking shelter in a relative's home. Camerado Jatin! I know that emptied cattle-yard as if I stood in it myself — the beasts you fed with your own hand, gone down in the brown water, and no fault of yours, and no help for it, only the relative's roof and the five of you crowded under it, waiting out the rain.

And I hear Sudip Mazumdar, a journalist of Guwahati, two million souls in that city and the water indifferent to the census. I had to stay overnight at my office, he says. The roads were filled with water, some waist deep. So it is not the paddy-field alone, not the thatch village alone — the paved street of the state capital stands drowned too, the commuter and the cultivator overtaken by the same river.

Where the helicopters go out with food and blankets over Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, Golaghat, Dibrugarh, Karbi Anglong, Kamrup, Nagaon, Dhemaji, Hojai — eleven districts named like a litany, each with its own drowned roads and its own dead — there the Chief Minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, stands and says plainly: I estimate that the casualty figure will rise further. This entire situation arose because of a cloudburst in Nagaland. One cloud, over a neighboring hill, and the water comes down a hundred miles to take a farmer's cattle and a journalist's sleep and fifty lives already counted and more not yet counted. Such is the arithmetic of a river.

Twenty-four thousand sheltering already in three hundred fifty-eight camps across nine districts; five thousand carried out by boat and by hand, the Army, the NDRF, the SDRF, the ordinary policeman wading to the elbow — and the Chief Minister owning, too, what is not yet done: The situation has improved slightly, but we still have not been able to reach around 20 per cent of the affected people. I would not soften that admission nor hide it in a parenthesis. Twenty in the hundred not yet reached is twenty in the hundred still standing on a roof, or a mound, or the last dry rise of ground, waiting.

I say this flood did not come only out of a cloud over Nagaland. I say a state that has known these waters since the great earthquake of 1950, that keeps forty-eight hundred kilometers of its own embankment and lets three-fifths of it fall into disrepair, that watched a twenty-eight per cent rainfall deficit and a drought in its own upper country the very month before this deluge — that state has been told, by its own engineers, in its own reports, that no long-term measures have been implemented, and has heard it and not built. The river does not read the report. The river only comes.

Yet the boats go out, and the airdrops fall, and the relative's door opens to the cattleless farmer, and the camps fill with the wet and the fed. Behind the water, and whatever it eventuations, the vital things remain — the hand that pulls another hand into the boat, the neighbor's floor given up to five strangers, the roads that will be walked again. I do not know when the Brahmaputra will lie back down in its bed. I know it has done this before, and that the people of Sivasagar and Nazira and Guwahati will still be there, in the mud, counting their own, when it does.
